data.title: Industrial content written by people who can read a spec sheet
paragraphs: There is no compliance officer waiting to catch the error here, only an engineer who stops reading at the first wrong number and decides your company does not know its own product.
We write for manufacturers whose buyers are technical, patient, and completely unforgiving of copy written by someone who has never seen the part.

data.title: What goes wrong when a generalist writes it
data.subtitle: The expensive mistakes in this field look like ordinary copy on the way out the door.

items.title: Specifications wrong in small ways
items.text: A tolerance, a material grade, or a unit converted carelessly, all of which the buyer notices immediately, and what they conclude has nothing to do with typos.
items.text2: A specifier checks the number against a datasheet before they call, so a wrong figure does not produce a question, it produces silence.

items.title: Copy written for the wrong reader
items.text: Consumer-style enthusiasm aimed at a specifier who wants dimensions, compatibility, and lead time, none of which warmth can supply.
items.text2: The specifier, the buyer and the person signing all read before anyone picks up the phone, and copy written for one of them leaves the other two without what they came for.

items.title: Certifications used as decoration
items.text: Standards and approvals listed as logos, when the claim is only useful once the reader knows what it lets them do.
items.text2: An approval is worth writing out, because a buyer who understands what it permits can carry it into their own meeting, and a logo gives them nothing to carry.

items.title: A long sales cycle treated as a short one
items.text: Industrial buying runs long and involves several people, so content written for one impulsive reader misses most of the room.
items.text2: Content that assumes a single decision misses the months in between, where the same page gets forwarded internally and has to answer someone outside the original audience.

data.title: What our writers already know
data.subtitle: A generalist looks this up once the draft is already due, and it is where a vertical writer starts.

items.title: Specifications and tolerances
items.text: Numbers, units, and materials handled precisely, because the reader checks.

items.title: Standards and certifications
items.text: What an approval permits, written so a specifier can use it and not merely see it.

items.title: Application and compatibility
items.text: Writing that answers whether this part works in that situation, which is what most industrial search is asking.

items.title: The technical buying committee
items.text: Content that speaks to the engineer, the buyer, and the person signing, because all three read before anyone calls.

items.title: Units, tolerances and conversions
items.text: Metric against imperial, nominal against actual, and the decimal place that turns a correct spec into a wrong one.

items.title: Lead time and availability language
items.text: What ships, what is built to order, and what is quoted, because getting vague here is how a technical buyer decides you do not know your own catalog.

data.title: Human writers, and an editor on every piece
paragraphs: Content Cucumber staffs human writers and puts an editor on every piece before it reaches you, so nothing arrives generated and handed over unread.

We assign writers to your account and keep them there, so the person writing in month six already carries your positions and your language, and you will know who is writing for you before the engagement starts.

data.title: Engineers care more than anyone admits

paragraphs: The reader who catches your wrong tolerance is the same reader with strong opinions about the machine on their floor, because this is a field full of pride, and writing that treats it as a commodity spec dump misses the person entirely.

Our writers bring enthusiasm to the work that deserves it, respect for a job that is hard to do well, and enough plain talk that an engineer does not feel marketed at. Precision earns you the read. Something to feel is what makes it worth finishing.

data.title: Found in AI search because an expert wrote it
data.subtitle: Answer engines quote passages they can lift without the passage falling apart, and vague copy does not clear that bar.

items.title: The answer comes first
items.text: Sections that open with the answer, which is the shape an engine can quote and a buyer can skim.

items.title: Specific enough to quote
items.text: Named detail and hard specifics, because a passage with nothing concrete in it gives a model nothing worth citing.

items.title: Written the way your buyer asks
items.text: A marketing lead at a manufacturer or industrial distributor searches in their own words, and the heading that matches the question is the one that gets surfaced.

items.title: Passages that stand alone
items.text: Each section holds up on its own, so a citation lands on something that still reads correctly out of context.

data.title: Your voice, and how the work ships
data.subtitle: We learn how you already sound, so the result reads as yours.

steps.title: We read what you publish
steps.text: Your recent published work, your brand guide if you have one, and the companies you get compared to, all of which becomes a style sheet the writers work from.

steps.title: We agree the topics
steps.text: Built from what you already surface for and the questions your buyers type, so the calendar belongs to you.

steps.title: A writer is assigned and stays
steps.text: The same people write for you month over month, so your positions carry forward from one brief to the next.

steps.title: An editor reads every piece
steps.text: Then it arrives on your schedule, ready to publish.

items.question: Do your writers have engineering backgrounds?
items.answer: We assign writers experienced with technical material, and we work from your specifications instead of paraphrasing them, and where a detail is properly technical we confirm it with you.

items.question: Can you write from our spec sheets and drawings?
items.answer: Yes, and we would rather work from those than from a marketing brief, because the source documents are what keep the numbers right.

items.question: Do you write product and category content at volume?
items.answer: Yes. Catalog-scale product copy is a different engagement from single deep pieces, and we will tell you which one you need.

items.question: Our field is niche. Is that a problem?
items.answer: It is usually an advantage, because narrow fields have less competent content in them, so accurate writing surfaces faster.
